title: Error Detection
tagline: Year 2 — Locating the grammatical error in a sentence divided into parts

introduction.overview: In an error-detection (spotting errors) question, a sentence is divided into three or four parts and you must find the part that contains a grammatical error, or say that there is no error. Because the answer is just the part and not a correction, the skill is rapid recognition of the common error types: agreement, tense, preposition, article, pronoun, adjective/adverb, comparison and word choice. A fixed checklist makes this reliable.
introduction.placementRelevance: Error-detection questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds, usually in sets of five.
introduction.realWorldContext: Proofreading emails, reports and presentations before sending uses the same checklist.

learningObjectives: Apply an error checklist in a fixed order
Spot subject-verb disagreement, including with phrases between subject and verb
Spot wrong prepositions, double comparatives and incorrect conjunctions
Spot errors in conditionals and reported speech

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Agreement, tense, preposition, article, pronoun case, adjective/adverb, comparison, conjunction, word order, redundancy.

coreDefinitions: Error detection: identifying the faulty part of a sentence without correcting it.
Part: a segment of the sentence marked A, B or C; option D usually reads "No error".
Common errors: agreement, tense, preposition, article, pronoun, comparison, conjunction.
Redundancy: needless repetition (return back, repeat again).
No error: the sentence is grammatically correct as written.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The error is usually small and sits in one word. Reading the sentence aloud in your head and then testing each part against the checklist is faster than rereading for "feel". About a fifth of such questions have no error, so do not assume every sentence is wrong.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Check in this order: subject and verb agreement, tense and verb form, prepositions and articles, pronouns, adjectives and adverbs, comparatives, conjunctions. Stop when you find the fault.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Agreement check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Find the real subject; match singular/plural
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Ignore phrases between subject and verb.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: The quality of the products has improved

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Form after helpers
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: do/does/did + V1; has/have/had + V3; to + V1 (but look forward to + -ing)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Fixed pairs
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: prefer X to Y; senior to; look forward to + -ing; despite (no of)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Conjunction pairs
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Although … (no but);  Hardly … when;  No sooner … than
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Although it rained, we went out

mainNarrative: Work through the checklist. Read each part and ask: does the verb agree with its subject? In "The children is playing", the plural subject children needs are. In "Each of the boys have a bicycle", the subject is each (singular), so has.
Check verb forms and fixed phrases. "He go to school" needs goes. "I look forward to meet you" needs meeting, because to is a preposition here. "She prefers tea than coffee" needs to coffee.
Check conjunctions and comparisons. "Although it rained, but we went out" has a double conjunction: remove but. "He is more smarter" has a double comparative.
Check reported speech and conditionals. "He asked me that where I lived" must be "He asked me where I lived". "If I would have known" must be "If I had known".
Finally, if every part passes the checklist, choose "No error". A sentence such as "Hardly had he arrived when the train left" is correct.

deepDiveAspects.title: Relative pronoun agreement
deepDiveAspects.content: "She is one of those who always arrives early": who refers to those (plural), so the verb should be arrive.

deepDiveAspects.title: As well as
deepDiveAspects.content: In "The teacher as well as the students was present", the verb agrees with the first subject, teacher, not with students.

solvedExamples.title: Agreement error
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: (A) The children (B) is playing (C) in the garden. (D) No error

steps.title: Verb
steps.explanation: "Is" is singular, so Part B is wrong: are playing.

solvedExamples.title: Fixed pair
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: (A) She prefers (B) tea than (C) coffee. (D) No error

steps.title: Pair
steps.explanation: The correct construction is prefer … to.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Prefer is followed by to, not than.

solvedExamples.title: No error
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: (A) Hardly had he arrived (B) when the (C) train left. (D) No error

steps.title: Check
steps.explanation: Hardly had + S + V3 + when is correct.

shortcutMethods.title: Checklist in order

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Agreement → verb form → preposition/article → pronoun → comparison → conjunction. Stop at the first fault; if none, choose No error.

rulesForApplication: Strike out phrases between subject and verb.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every sentence has an error

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing the word near the error.
Reading the phrase near the verb.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Mark parts that pass the checklist and eliminate them.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Five common errors cover most questions.

easy.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) He go  (B) to school  (C) every day.  (D) No error
easy.explanation: "He" is third person singular, so the verb should be goes.

easy.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) The children  (B) is playing  (C) in the garden.  (D) No error
easy.explanation: Children is plural, so are playing.

easy.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) She has  (B) a good  (C) knowledges.  (D) No error
easy.explanation: Knowledge is uncountable and has no plural form.

intermediate.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) Neither of the two  (B) answers are  (C) correct.  (D) No error
intermediate.explanation: Neither is singular, so the verb should be is.

intermediate.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) Hardly had he arrived  (B) when the  (C) train left.  (D) No error
intermediate.explanation: The sentence is correct: Hardly had … when.

intermediate.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) I look forward  (B) to meet  (C) you soon.  (D) No error
intermediate.explanation: After look forward to, use -ing: meeting.

advanced.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) If I  (B) would have known,  (C) I would have told you.  (D) No error
advanced.explanation: Type 3 conditional: if I had known.

advanced.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) The quality of  (B) the products  (C) have improved.  (D) No error
advanced.explanation: The subject quality is singular, so has improved.

placementStyle.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) She has been  (B) living here  (C) since 2010.  (D) No error
placementStyle.explanation: The present perfect continuous with since is correct.

placementStyle.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) Between you  (B) and I,  (C) the plan is risky.  (D) No error
placementStyle.explanation: After a preposition use me: between you and me.

placementStyle.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
(A) He is more  (B) smarter  (C) than his brother.  (D) No error
placementStyle.explanation: Double comparative: smarter than, or more intelligent than.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I spot a double conjunction?
Can I spot a wrong fixed pair?
Can I recognise a correct sentence?

sourcesAndReferences.sourceName: High School English Grammar and Composition — Wren & Martin
